task: Matrix sparsification: given the operator U of a fast multiplication algorithm, find an invertible V minimising nnz(U V)
source: Produced by `reproduce/measure.py`, which runs `sparsify-operator fixtures/<name>.matrix` once per operator.
why: Fewer nonzeros in the operator means fewer additions in the algorithm it encodes, which is the cost the multiplication count does not capture.
machine: Single core of a 12th Gen Intel i5-12450H at 2.2 GHz.
methods: Exact, matroid greedy over Q: scan column supports in ascending size and keep every codeword that raises the rank. The minimum over every invertible V, by Rado-Edmonds, and the only method here proved so.

The three methods removed on 2026-08-22 (row-basis heuristic, and both of [beniamini2020]'s oracles) reached the same counts 88x to 343x more slowly and are on the dominated-methods branch, with their measurements; see matrix_sparsification/dominated.md.
readings: The strand has a number now. Strassen's two encoding operators go from 12 nonzeros to 10; the alternative-basis operator goes from 21 to 10. All three methods reach the same 10, and every result is checked to have the same row space as the operator it came from.

Ten is what the row-basis construction predicts rather than a surprise: inverting a square block of rows makes four rows singletons, and the remaining three come out with two nonzeros each. It is not proved minimal, and none of these methods proves anything minimal.
The runs take milliseconds because field operations on small matrices (7×4) are cheap compared to the minimisation over a discrete space.

The operators no longer have to be typed in. The rank search recovers L and R from the decomposition it finds and writes them out, so deriving a fast algorithm and then reducing its additions is two commands. On F2 5x5 that is 25 multiplications down to 14, and the left operator's 31 nonzeros down to 27.
corrections: Algorithm 2.4 was unreachable. Both branches of the prompt that offers the choice call algorithm 2.3, so the top-down oracle could never run from the command line.
Its search returns None when it finds no candidate, into a caller that unpacks the result into two variables. It does not fire on these operators, so it was latent rather than observed.

The search objective counts zeros exactly by testing field equality, not floating-point equality. Using `== 0` on raw doubles can miscount: on the alternative-basis operator this sees 86 zeros where 144 exist, even with post-rounding applied. The reported count can be sound while the objective being maximised is not.
limits: The matroid greedy over Q returns the minimum and stops on collecting a basis rather than on a proof that nothing lighter exists, so it does not finish on an operator whose greedy weights are large: 4x4x4_49_156_L needs weight 6 or more for 7 of its 16 vectors, where the scan is 14 million column subsets rising to 451 million at weight 8. That operator's column matroid does look regular, and there the minimum weight is a linear programme rather than a search: see matrix_sparsification/method/when-the-matroid-is-regular.md, which reaches a 16-vector basis at 100 nonzeros in 0.08 s with its first nine weights proved optimal. The greedy by rescaling, behind --operations, guarantees nothing and minimises nnz + nns rather than nnz, which is why speed does not order it against the rest.
